title: The July Visa Bulletin Just Shut the Door on India's EB-2 Green Cards. It Will Not Reopen Until October.
excerpt: EB-2 India declared unavailable for the rest of FY2026, EB-1 retrogressed by two months, and EB-5 unreserved also shut — the worst mid-year bulletin for Indian professionals in years.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • EB-2 category for Indian applicants is now marked 'Unavailable' until October 2026.
  • EB-1 category has retrogressed by two months, now at October 15, 2022.
  • Approximately 400,000 Indian nationals are affected by the EB-2 freeze.
  • Legislative reform is urgently needed to address the backlog and per-country cap.
  • Indian professionals face the longest wait times for green cards compared to other countries.

U.S. State Department Visa Bulletin
The U.S. State Department's July 2026 Visa Bulletin has delivered a blow that hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals have been dreading: the Employment-Based Second Preference (EB-2) category is now marked "Unavailable" for Indian applicants. No new green cards will be issued in this category until the new fiscal year begins on October 1. It is the most significant mid-year retrogression for India in recent memory, and it comes at a time when the backlog of Indian EB-2 applicants — engineers, doctors, researchers, technology professionals — runs into the hundreds of thousands. This development is particularly disheartening for the Indian diaspora, many of whom have built their lives and careers in the U.S. and now face an extended period of uncertainty regarding their permanent residency. ## What the July Bulletin Says The headline numbers are stark. EB-2 India, which had a final action date of September 1, 2013 last month, is now listed as "U" — unavailable. The State Department, in its official bulletin, stated that "high demand and number use by Indian applicants" made it necessary to shut the category entirely to stay within the fiscal year's annual limit. EB-1 India, typically the fastest lane for multinational executives and individuals with extraordinary ability, has retrogressed by two months. The final action date is now October 15, 2022. The department warned that further retrogression — or even making EB-1 unavailable — could become necessary if India's allotted share is exhausted before the fiscal year ends on September 30. EB-3 India, the third preference category for skilled workers, has advanced modestly to January 1, 2014, a half-month gain. However, with final action dates stuck more than twelve years in the past, the practical relief for most applicants is negligible. The unreserved EB-5 investor visa category for India has also been declared unavailable, after its annual quota was exhausted. Only the EB-5 set-aside categories — rural, high unemployment area, and infrastructure — remain current. USCIS has confirmed that employment-based applicants must use the Final Action Dates chart to determine filing eligibility in July, meaning the retrogression and unavailability hit applicants directly where it hurts most: the ability to file or have adjudicated their I-485 adjustment of status applications. ## What This Means for Indian Professionals For the roughly 400,000 Indian nationals in the EB-2 queue — many of whom have lived and worked in the United States for a decade or more on H-1B visas — the bulletin means their green card applications are frozen for at least three more months. No new EB-2 cases will be approved until the FY2027 allocation begins in October. This prolonged wait can impact everything from career progression to family planning for these individuals and their families. Those with pending I-485 applications are not deported, but they cannot receive final green card approval. Their Employment Authorization Documents (EADs) and Advance Parole travel documents remain valid as long as the underlying petition is pending, but travel carries risks: re-entry on Advance Parole during a period of unavailability can create complications. For applicants considering a job change, the AC21 portability provision still applies if their I-485 has been pending for 180 days or more. But any applicant who has not yet filed I-485 and whose priority date falls after the now-frozen cutoff has no path to file until dates advance again. Immigration attorneys across the country have noted a sharp increase in inquiries about EB-3 downgrading — a strategy where EB-2 applicants refile under EB-3, which is backlogged but at least still moving. The trade-off is real: EB-3 India's final action date is January 2014, which may actually be ahead of some applicants' EB-2 priority dates. This strategy, while offering a glimmer of hope, often involves additional legal fees and further delays.
Legislative Challenges for Indian Professionals
›Per-country cap limits visas to 7% for each nation.
›India and China account for most EB applications.
›Legislative proposals like the EAGLE Act have stalled.
›Indian EB-2 backlog could stretch to decades without reform.
## The Structural Problem The root cause remains unchanged: the per-country cap that limits each nation to roughly seven per cent of employment-based immigrant visas, regardless of demand. India and China together account for the vast majority of EB applications, but receive the same annual allocation as countries that file a fraction of the petitions. This disproportionate allocation creates immense backlogs for high-demand countries. Multiple legislative proposals to eliminate or raise the per-country cap — including the bipartisan EAGLE Act — have stalled in Congress over the past several years. Without legislative reform, immigration lawyers say the Indian EB-2 backlog will continue to grow, potentially stretching wait times to several decades for new applicants. The contrast with other countries is sharp. EB-1 and EB-2 remain "Current" for applicants from most countries. Even China, which faces its own significant backlog, has EB-2 final action dates at September 2021 — nearly eight years ahead of where India stood before the category went unavailable. ## The Diaspora Angle For Indian Americans and the broader NRI community, the bulletin reinforces a painful reality: the United States remains the most difficult country in the world for Indian professionals to obtain permanent residency, despite being the country where they contribute the most to the economy. Indian immigrants have founded 96 billion-dollar startups in America and earn the highest median household income of any immigrant group. And yet many face a two-decade wait for the same green card that applicants from other countries receive in months. This disparity not only impacts individual lives but also affects the ability of the U.S. to retain top talent. The July bulletin's triple blow — EB-2 unavailable, EB-1 retrogressing, EB-5 unreserved shut — makes the case for legislative reform more urgent than ever. However, with Congress focused on other priorities and the current political climate, meaningful change remains elusive. This situation can lead to talented Indian professionals considering other countries for permanent settlement, impacting the U.S. economy and its innovation landscape. The next Visa Bulletin, for August, will be closely watched. If EB-1 India follows EB-2 into unavailability, it would leave Indian professionals with virtually no employment-based path to permanent residency for the remainder of the fiscal year — an unprecedented situation for the country that sends more skilled workers to America than any other.
